summary: Religious experts from Jerusalem object that Jesus's disciples eat without the ritual handwashing. He answers hard — quoting Isaiah at them and giving an example where a religious rule was being used to cut off support to aging parents — then tells the crowd that nothing entering a person from outside can defile them. Mark adds a note that this made all foods clean. Jesus then leaves Jewish territory entirely, is out-argued by a Gentile woman who wants her daughter freed, and heals a deaf man in the Decapolis.
whyItMatters: This chapter dismantles the boundary between clean and unclean, and then immediately walks across it. The argument about food is followed by Jesus going to Tyre and the Decapolis and helping people that argument would have excluded. Mark puts the theory and the practice side by side.

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching
context.audience: Non-Jewish readers — verses 3-4 stop the narrative to explain Jewish washing customs, which no Jewish reader would need
context.setting: Galilee, then the Gentile regions of Tyre and Sidon on the Mediterranean coast, then back through the Decapolis
context.literaryForm: A controversy story with an explanation attached, followed by two healings placed to make the argument concrete

outline.heading: The handwashing complaint
outline.note: With Mark's parenthesis explaining the custom to outsiders

outline.heading: Tradition against commandment
outline.note: Isaiah quoted, then the Corban example — a vow used to avoid supporting parents

outline.heading: What actually defiles
outline.note: Said publicly as a riddle, explained privately; Mark draws the conclusion in verse 19

outline.heading: The Syrophoenician woman
outline.note: He tries to stay hidden, gives a hard answer, and she answers it

outline.heading: Ephphatha
outline.note: A deaf man in Gentile territory; fingers, spit, a sigh, and one Aramaic word

keyVerses.text: For you set aside the commandment of God, and hold tightly to the tradition of men
keyVerses.why: The charge in one line — not that they have too many rules, but that the rules have started overriding the thing they were built to protect.

keyVerses.text: There is nothing from outside of the man that going into him can defile him; but the things which proceed out of the man are those that defile the man.
keyVerses.why: The sentence that relocates purity from the body to the will.

keyVerses.text: Yes, Lord. Yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.
keyVerses.why: The only time in the gospels anyone wins an exchange with Jesus — and he says so.

keyVerses.text: He has done all things well. He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!
keyVerses.why: A Gentile crowd's verdict, echoing Isaiah 35:5-6 about what happens when God comes to rescue.

questions.question: Was handwashing before meals actually a law?
questions.answer: Not in the written law for ordinary people — the Hebrew scriptures require it of priests handling holy things. What developed was a practice of extending priestly purity into everyday life, so that ordinary meals were treated with something of the care given to temple service. Mark calls it 'the tradition of the elders,' which is precisely the distinction Jesus goes on to press. This was a devout impulse, not a petty one, which is what makes the argument serious.

questions.question: Verses 3-4 read like a footnote. Why is that there?
questions.answer: Because Mark is writing for people who do not know any of this. A Jewish reader would find the explanation redundant to the point of being odd. Small asides like this one are among the strongest internal clues about who this book was for — and they sit alongside his habit of translating Aramaic. Both point the same direction: an audience outside Judea that did not speak the language or keep the customs.

questions.question: What is Corban, and what is the abuse being described?
questions.answer: Corban means dedicated to God. Mark translates it for his readers in verse 11. The practice under attack: a man declares his property or income Corban, which puts it out of reach for ordinary use — and then cites that dedication as the reason he cannot support his aging parents. A vow with a religious label is being used to get out of the fifth commandment. Jesus's point is not that vows are bad, but that a rule which lets you dodge 'honour your father and mother' has inverted its own purpose.

questions.question: Is Jesus against tradition as such?
questions.answer: Read carefully, he attacks a specific failure mode, not tradition generally. His complaint is that a human tradition has been allowed to void a clear command from God, and he names the mechanism. He argues by quoting scripture, which is itself a traditional move, and elsewhere he keeps festivals and teaches in synagogues. The test he applies is whether the practice still serves what it was built to serve — the same test as 2:27 about the Sabbath.

questions.question: Verse 19 says 'making all foods clean.' Is that Jesus speaking or Mark?
questions.answer: It is Mark's own comment on what Jesus said, not part of the quotation — most modern translations set it off, and this one does too. It matters because it is a rare moment where Mark steps in to tell you the implication. He is writing for a mixed community where whether Gentile believers had to keep Jewish food laws was a live and painful question, as Acts 10 and Galatians 2 both show. Mark is telling his readers where he thinks that question was settled.

questions.question: Why does Jesus call the woman's people 'dogs'? That sounds cruel.
questions.answer: It is the hardest sentence in the chapter and no reading makes it comfortable. What can be said: the word used is not the term for a street scavenger but a diminutive, closer to a household dog under the table — which is the opening she takes. His actual statement is about order, 'let the children be filled first,' and Mark has him already sitting in Gentile territory having gone there deliberately. Some read it as a genuine statement of mission priority that she successfully challenges. Some read it as a deliberate opening offered to be taken. Others hold that it is simply a hard saying and refuse to soften it. Mark records the exchange without smoothing it, and records that she wins.

questions.question: Does she actually change his mind?
questions.answer: Mark's wording is direct: 'For this saying, go your way.' The reason given for the healing is her answer. Whatever else is happening, this is the one conversation in the gospels that Jesus concedes — to a foreign woman with no standing to press him, in someone else's country. It is also worth noticing where Mark has placed it: immediately after the argument that nothing outside a person can defile them.

questions.question: Why the fingers, the spit, and the sigh? It seems oddly physical.
questions.answer: Elsewhere Jesus heals with a word, so the difference is worth noticing. The gestures are legible to a man who cannot hear a word of explanation — fingers to the ears, touch to the tongue, a look upward to say where this is coming from. It is communication in the only channel available. The sigh Mark records without interpreting; readers usually take it as grief at the damage being addressed.

questions.question: Why is the route in verse 31 so strange?
questions.answer: It is a long way round — from Tyre north to Sidon, then southeast to the lake through the Decapolis. People have argued about whether Mark knew the geography. The most straightforward reading is that the route is the point: Jesus spends an extended stretch in Gentile territory, and the two healings in this chapter both happen out there. Coming right after the food argument, the itinerary is part of the argument.

questions.question: Why does he keep telling people not to talk, when it never works?
questions.answer: Verse 36 is almost comic about it — the more he ordered them, the more they spread it. Mark seems aware of the futility and reports it anyway. It fits the wider pattern: the reputation Jesus is trying not to build is exactly the one that makes it harder to say what he actually came to do. Notice these orders stop after the crucifixion, when the thing that was being protected has happened.

glossary.def: Accumulated oral rulings on how to apply the written law in daily life. Highly respected, and distinct from scripture itself — which is the distinction under argument here.
Ritually unfit to approach worship. In this chapter Jesus moves the source of defilement from what touches the outside of a person to what comes out of them.
Aramaic for 'dedicated to God.' Mark translates it in the text. A vow that set property apart — and, in the abuse described, put it beyond the reach of an obligation to parents.
Originally a Greek stage term for an actor. The image is of a performance, which is why it pairs with the Isaiah quotation about lips and hearts.
A Gentile woman from the coastal region of Phoenicia in the Roman province of Syria. Mark also calls her Greek — meaning Greek-speaking and pagan, not Greek by descent.
Aramaic for 'be opened.' Mark preserves the word and translates it, as he does elsewhere.
